metadata.title: Non-Perturbative Nuclear Equation of State and Relativistic Neutron Star Mass-Radius Limits in Unified Phase Dynamics: Testing Against NASA NICER and Gravitational-Wave Tidal Deformability
metadata.description:
Understanding the equation of state (EOS) of dense nuclear matter at supranuclear densities (ρ > ρ0 ≈ 2.7 × 1014 g/cm3, ϵ0 ≈ 150 MeV/fm3) represents one of the foremost open problems in relativistic astrophysics. NASA's NICER X-ray pulse-profile modeling has established that neutron stars maintain an almost constant radius of R ≈ 12.4 km across 1.4 M⊙ ≤ M ≤ 2.1 M⊙ (PSR J0030+0451: R = 12.45 ± 0.65 km; PSR J0740+6620: R = 12.39 ± 0.98 km; PSR J0437-4715: R ∈ [11.36, 12.50] km), while LIGO-Virgo GW170817 constrains the dimensionless tidal deformability to Λ1.4 ∈ [70, 580].

In the framework of the Unified Phase Dynamics of Feynman Path Contours, dense matter is derived from non-perturbative center vortex condensation in SU(3)c. An entire Schwinger contour form factor Ε(&Box;) = exp(-smin2&Box;2 / ℏ2) introduces a topological phase stiffness above nuclear saturation, producing a speed of sound peak (cs2 ≈ 0.52 at ∼ 1.9 ϵ0) that asymptotically relaxes to the conformal limit cs2 → 1/3 at ultra-high deconfined densities.

Integrating the relativistic Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) stellar structure and quadrupole tidal Love number equations yields:

  • Canonical 1.4 M⊙ Radius: R1.4 = 12.67 km (within 0.34σ of NICER PSR J0030+0451);
  • Massive 2.08 M⊙ Radius: R2.08 = 13.92 km (within 1.56σ of NICER PSR J0740+6620);
  • Maximum Stable Mass: Mmax = 2.58 M⊙ (R(Mmax) = 14.02 km), resolving the nature of the secondary component of GW190814 (M ≈ 2.50–2.67 M⊙) without requiring black hole collapse;
  • Tidal Deformability: Λ1.4 = 245.7 (in perfect concordance with the LIGO-Virgo GW170817 90% credible interval).

This zero-parameter deductive derivation reconciles soft low-density crusts with ultra-stiff cores, proving that relativistic neutron star structure is governed by non-perturbative topological phase holonomies.
